In general, if M is representable, we conjecture that the combinatorial derived matroid is generic in two different ways; one categorical and one algebraic-geometric. In order to state Conjectures 8.5 and 8.6, we need some auxiliary standard definitions.
Definition 8.4.
Let E be a finite set. The weak order the class ℳ of matroids with ground set E is the partial order with M1≥M2 if every dependent set in M1 is also dependent in M2.
Conjecture 8.5.
Let M be a representable matroid on ground set E. Then δ⁡(M)≥δO​W​(R) for every representation R of M, where the order relation is the weak order on the set of matroids on E.
Note that Lemma 8.2 proves Conjecture 8.5 in the case that δ​M=(𝒞,𝒜0). It is conceivable that Conjecture 8.5 may be approached with techniques similar to those in [6]. There, the authors studied conditions under which the collection a matroids with some circuits prescribed have a maximal element in the weak order.
For algebraic-geometric notions of genericity, fix a field 𝔽 and let 𝔽¯ be its algebraic closure. Assume that M is representable over 𝔽, with |E⁡(M)|=n and r⁡(M)=k. We can then define the variety V⁡(M)=V𝔽​(M)⊆𝔽¯k×n of matrices that represent M. This is clearly an algebraic variety, since it is defined by the vanishing of certain finitely many minors and the non-vanishing of finitely many others. We also have a variety V⁡(N)⊆𝔽¯(n−k)×|𝒞| for every possible 𝔽¯-representable matroid N on the ground set 𝒞=𝒞⁡(M). Then the map
R↦δ⁡(R)
subdivides V⁡(M) into components
VN​(M)={R∈V⁡(M):δO​W​(R)=N},
for different possible Oxley–Wang derived matroids N of M. From this perspective, genericity is captured by the following conjecture.
Conjecture 8.6.
For every matroid N≠δ⁡(M) on 𝒞, VN​(M) has positive codimension in V⁡(M).
Since there are only finitely many possible Oxley–Wang derived matroids, this would imply that Vδ⁡(M)​(M) would be a full-dimensional subvariety of V⁡(M). In particular, assume that 𝔽 is a finite field and that 𝔽′/𝔽 is a finite field extension whose degree [𝔽′:𝔽] tends to infinity. Conjecture 8.6 would then imply that asymptotically almost all representations R of M over 𝔽′ would satisfy δO​W​(R)=δ​(M).
8.2 Adjoint
The construction of the combinatorial derived matroid is iterative. However, there are sets for which we can directly say if they are dependent or independent in δ​M, without going through the iterative process. Given a set, we first check the nullity condition (3) in Definition 4.3. If this condition is satisfied, the set is in 𝒜0 hence dependent. If not, we check if the set satisfies condition (6) in Corollary 6.5 about the support. If this condition is satisfied, the set is independent. In case a set satisfies neither condition (3) nor (6), the only way to check its (in)dependence is by constructing iteratively all dependent sets of δ​M and see if our set is one of them.
The fact that there are sets for which (in)dependence is hard to check, means it is also difficult to define a closure function of δ​M. We are not optimistic about finding a definition of closure in δ​M without some form of iteration.
As a result of the lack of closure in δ​M, we have not managed to compare the definition of δ​M, that uses dependent sets, to that of the adjoint (Section 3.4), that uses closed sets. We expect the following to be true.
Conjecture 8.7.
If an adjoint of a matroid exist, one of them is equal to the combinatorial derived matroid of the dual.
Duality in this conjecture follows from the fact that the complement of a closed set is a union of cocircuits, see also the discussion at the end of Section 3.3. Towards settling the conjecture, we present some results on closure in the combinatorial derived matroid.

Let S⊆𝒞 and C∈S¯−S. Then for all inclusion-maximal independent sets I⊆S, C∈I¯−I.
